name: Fedora

card.summary: The fedora is a brimmed felt hat with a creased crown that finishes an outfit and frames the face, worn by men and women since the late 1800s.

quick.overview:
A fedora is a soft felt hat with a lengthwise crease in the crown, a pinch at the front and a brim of about 2.5 inches. It is a style accessory: it adds a finished, classic look to an outfit and can frame the face and shade the eyes.

The hat has a long fashion history, peaking from the 1920s to the early 1950s, and has had revivals in the 21st century. No studies have tested its effect on attractiveness; it is documented here as a style item with a long record in menswear and film.
quick.how: People wear fedoras as part of a coordinated outfit, choosing a brim width, crown shape and colour (black, brown and grey are the most common) to suit face shape and clothing. Variations include teardrop, diamond and center-dent crowns, and rollable or crushable versions. Sizing and brim angle are matters of fit and taste.
quick.risks: There are no medical risks. Hats can flatten hair, and a poorly fitted or mismatched hat can look out of place; some communities also attach a stereotype to the fedora in internet culture.

lead: A fedora is a felt hat with a soft brim and an indented crown, usually creased lengthwise and pinched at the front. A typical crown is about 4.5 inches (11 cm) tall and the brim about 2.5 inches (6.4 cm) wide, and the hat is commonly made of wool, rabbit or beaver felt, with straw, cotton, linen and leather versions also made.[1]

People wear it to finish an outfit. The hat adds a defined, vintage-leaning silhouette, frames the face, shades the eyes and gives a head of hair a deliberate, put-together outline. Brim width, crown height, colour and band are the main choices: black, brown and grey are the most common colours, and men's fedoras often have the brim turned down in front and up at the back.[1][2] The shorter 'stingy brim' and wider 'optimo' brims, and the narrower-brimmed trilby, give different proportions on the face.[2][3]

The name comes from Victorien Sardou's play Fédora, which premiered in Paris on 11 December 1882 with Sarah Bernhardt in the lead and a soft creased hat that women adopted as a fashion.[4][1] The hat passed into men's wardrobes from the 1890s, was a standard business and street accessory through the 1940s, faded from the late 1950s as dress became more casual, and has returned in revivals since the early 2000s.[1][2] It is associated with Humphrey Bogart, Frank Sinatra, Indiana Jones and Michael Jackson, and in internet culture it also carries a stereotype of its own.[1][5]

paras: The standard fedora has a creased crown, a pinch at the front, an angled brim and a ribbon band between crown and brim. Crowns run about 4 to 6 inches and brims about 2 to 4 inches; the brim is soft and can be worn flat or snapped up or down.[1][2] A sweatband inside is sized to head circumference, with common hat sizes running from about 6 7/8 to 7 1/2.[2]

Fedoras are made by pressing felt over a mold with heat or a sealant to hold the shape. Early makers used wooden blocks and irons; modern makers use metal molds and machinery.[1] Brim edges may be raw, sewn with a welt or bound with ribbon trim, and a hand-finished Cavanagh edge with near-invisible stitching is a costly treatment that needs a skilled craftsperson.[1]

Crown shapes include the teardrop, diamond and center-dent, and there are rollable, crushable and ventilated versions with grommets or mesh inlets.[1] Wool, cashmere, rabbit and beaver felt are the traditional materials, sometimes blended with mink or chinchilla, while straw, cotton, hemp and linen versions are worn in warm weather.[1] Contemporary designs include asymmetrical brims, bright colours and patterns, though neutral, simple styles remain the most common.[1]

Wikipedia describes the trilby as a narrow-brimmed hat whose brim is angled down at the front and slightly turned up at the back, with a somewhat lower crown than a fedora; the fedora's brim is wider and more level.[3][1] The homburg has a stiffer, curled brim.[2] The trilby takes its name from the 1895 London stage adaptation of George du Maurier's 1894 novel Trilby.[3]

Style writers and the traditions of menswear treat the hat as an accessory chosen to match the outfit. It was traditionally paired with business suits, and neutral tones are the usual recommendation for everyday wear.[2] The angle of the brim changes the impression: Grokipedia notes that a tilted brim is read as suggesting mystery and authority.[2]

The brim also frames the upper face and casts shade over the eyes, which people use to soften or sharpen the look of the forehead and brow. Wearers match brim width and crown height to head size and build, which is a matter of taste rather than a measured rule. Fit matters in the same way as for any tailored item: a hat sized to the head sits level, while a loose one slips and a tight one marks the forehead.[2]
Care advice commonly given for felt hats includes brushing off dust, steaming to restore the crease and avoiding moisture, which can warp or shrink wool felt.[2]

The term was in use by 1891. Sardou's play, written for Sarah Bernhardt, premiered at the Théâtre du Vaudeville on 11 December 1882 and reached the United States in 1889; Bernhardt wore a center-creased, soft-brimmed hat in it, and women's rights activists later took the style up as a symbol.[1][4]

After Edward, Prince of Wales (later the Duke of Windsor), began wearing one in 1924, the hat became popular with men.[1] During the 1910s and 1920s its popularity grew alongside the derby and the homburg. In the 1940s American brims widened while British brims stayed slightly smaller, and wartime colours such as khaki, blue and green joined the traditional black, brown and grey.[1]

Sears, Bailey, Borsalino and Stetson were prominent makers and sellers.[1] John B. Stetson founded his Philadelphia company in 1865, and by 1886 it was reportedly the largest hat maker in the world; the company closed its Philadelphia factory in 1971 and moved to licensing.[6]

Wikipedia places the hat's decline in the late 1950s, as men's dress became more informal.[1] Grokipedia adds that it declined after World War II amid casual dress, car travel and youth rebellion, and that John F. Kennedy's bare-headed 1961 inauguration further diminished it.[2] The trilby similarly peaked in the late 1950s and early 1960s, partly because low head clearance in postwar American cars made tall crowns impractical, and faded around 1970.[3]

sections.h: In film, music and public life
paras: Film noir made the fedora a staple of detectives and criminals. Humphrey Bogart wore one in The Maltese Falcon (1941) and The Big Sleep (1946), and Prohibition-era gangsters and zoot suit fashion tied it to a tough-guy image.[1] Al Capone was often photographed in a Stetson playboy style.[1]

Tom Landry wore one as head coach of the Dallas Cowboys from 1960 to 1988 and it became his trademark; Harrison Ford's Indiana Jones in Raiders of the Lost Ark wore a Herbert Johnson felt fedora and is credited with reviving the style; Michael Jackson wore one on stage, including in Smooth Criminal; and Tom Baker wore one as the Fourth Doctor in Doctor Who.[1] The Blues Brothers wore black fedoras, and Billy Wilder directed a 1978 film titled Fedora.[1]

Many Haredi and Orthodox Jewish men wear black fedoras daily, with Borsalino-type models common in some communities.[1][2] Frank Sinatra is more closely identified with the trilby, and a signature design bears his name.[3]

By the early 21st century the fedora was seen as a hipster symbol; Vice called the early 2000s a 'fedora renaissance' with celebrities such as Johnny Depp wearing one, and a 2007 article described it making a comeback against the baseball cap.[1] The trilby likewise became a favourite of hipster subculture in the 1990s and 2000s and briefly returned as a fashion item in the late 2000s and early 2010s.[3]

In internet culture the hat also became a stereotype. Wikipedia's article on the 'neckbeard' slang term describes a mocked type of man who identifies with nerd, gamer or geek subcultures, and links it to internet commentary from 2014 to 2016 in outlets including GQ and Vox.[5] Grokipedia lists the 'fedora tipper' meme, associated with a stereotype of insincere chivalry, among the hat's modern associations.[2]

Wearers who like the hat point to its long record on figures from Bogart to Sinatra. No study has measured how the hat affects the way people are perceived, so both the stereotype and the classic image rest on cultural association.

A hat carries no medical risk. Practical points described in style and hat-care sources are that hats can flatten hair, that wool felt can warp or shrink when wet, and that a hat that does not match the outfit or fit the head can look out of place.[2] Some fedoras use fur felts such as beaver or rabbit, which matters to people who avoid animal products; straw, cotton and other fabric versions exist.[1]

timeline.event: John B. Stetson founds his hat company in Philadelphia.[6]
Sardou's Fédora premieres in Paris with Sarah Bernhardt; her soft creased hat gives the style its name.[4]
The play reaches the United States.[1]
George du Maurier's novel Trilby is published; the 1895 London play gives the trilby its name.[3]
Edward, Prince of Wales, begins wearing a fedora, popularising it among men.[1]
Humphrey Bogart wears one in The Maltese Falcon.[1]
Tom Landry begins coaching the Dallas Cowboys in a fedora, a trademark until 1988.[1]
Kennedy's bare-headed inauguration is cited as a further blow to men's hat-wearing.[2]
Stetson closes its Philadelphia factory and shifts to licensing.[6]
Raiders of the Lost Ark, with Harrison Ford's Herbert Johnson fedora, is released.[1]
A 'fedora renaissance' is described in the press.[1]

lore.intro: The fedora is discussed in style communities as a classic accessory and, separately, as an internet stereotype. The claims below are about its look and reception.[1][5]

claims.claim: A fedora adds a classic, finished look to an outfit.
claims.believers: Wearers and style writers describe it as a defined silhouette that frames the face and suits suits, coats and casual wear when the colour is neutral.[1][2]
claims.experts: No study has tested the effect of a fedora on perceived attractiveness; the evidence is the hat's long documented place in menswear.[1]

claims.claim: The wrong hat or fit makes a person look worse.
claims.believers: Style advice holds that brim width, crown height and fit should suit head size and outfit, and that mismatched hats look costume-like.[2]
claims.experts: There are no published fit or proportion studies for hats; guidance comes from tailoring and hat-making tradition.[2]

claims.claim: The fedora carries a negative internet stereotype.
claims.believers: Commentators describe a 'fedora tipper' type and associate the hat with the neckbeard caricature.[2][5]
claims.experts: Wikipedia traces the neckbeard label to 2014 to 2016 press such as GQ and Vox; no research measures how strangers react to the hat itself.[5]

claims.claim: The trilby is a smaller, safer version of the fedora.
claims.believers: Retailers and writers describe the narrower brim and lower crown as more modern and less dramatic.[3]
claims.experts: Hat references describe the trilby as having a shorter, angled brim and lower crown; the 'safer' judgement is taste.[3]

claims.believers: A popular account credits Kennedy's bare-headed 1961 inauguration with ending men's hats.[2]
claims.experts: Wikipedia attributes the decline to more informal dress from the late 1950s, and the trilby article also cites low car roofs.[1][3]

claims.claim: The hat flatters particular face shapes.
claims.believers: Style guides suggest wider brims to balance larger faces and narrower brims for slighter ones.[2]
claims.experts: No studies test hat shape against face shape; the advice is convention.[2]
